scams.name: Beach Grab / Swim-and-Steal
scams.description: You wade into the Mediterranean off Promenade des Anglais for a quick swim, leaving your bag on the pebbles. Minutes later, someone who has been watching from a bench a hundred meters away walks past, scoops up the bag, and is gone before you dry off. The private beach clubs are no safer — thieves pay the entry fee and work the loungers while paying customers sleep.
scams.avoidance: Take only what you can hold in a waterproof pouch into the water. Leave passport, cards, and phone in your hotel safe. If you sunbathe, use your bag as a pillow rather than leaving it on top of your towel. Travel with a companion and swim in shifts so someone is always watching the gear.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais beach, Public beaches, Private beach clubs

scams.name: Taxi Meter Manipulation / Overcharging
scams.description: Nice taxi drivers have a long-running reputation for working tourists over at the airport and train station. Drivers claim the meter is broken, quote inflated flat rates, cover the meter with a hand, or take the long route through Promenade des Anglais traffic. Many refuse credit cards and skip the legally required receipt. Official fixed rates: airport to Nice center €32, airport to Cannes €85, airport to Monaco €95.
scams.avoidance: Know the fixed rates before you land. Confirm the price before you get in, and insist on the meter for any non-fixed route. Use Uber or Bolt when you want tracked, transparent pricing. Ask for a receipt every time — drivers who refuse are the ones worth reporting.
scams.location: Nice Airport, Train Station (Gare de Nice-Ville), Hotel pickups, Tourist areas

scams.name: Airport Tram Ticket Overcharge
scams.description: The ticket machines at Nice Airport sell only a special ‘airport ticket’ priced at €10 round trip — roughly three times the regular tram fare of €1.70. The machines don’t advertise the cheaper option, and most tourists pay the premium because they don’t know one exists.
scams.avoidance: Walk one stop to Grand Arenas, where the machines sell the regular €1.70 fare. Better still, buy on the Lignes d’Azur mobile app before you even leave the terminal. The tram is the same; only the ticket costs six times more if you buy it where the tourists do.
scams.location: Nice Côte d’Azur Airport, Airport tram terminals

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: A stranger bends down near you along Promenade des Anglais, picks up what looks like a gold ring, and asks if you dropped it. When you say no, they show you the ’14k’ stamp and insist it must be valuable. They offer to sell it for a fraction of its ‘worth,’ or press it into your hand and demand a finder’s fee. The ring is brass worth pennies — and while you’re engaging, an accomplice is often working your pockets.
scams.avoidance: Say *non* and keep walking without slowing down. Do not touch the ring — the moment you hold it, they pivot to pressure. Keep hands on your bag or in your pockets. Scan for the second player: ring scams almost always run with an accomplice.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Old Town (Vieux Nice), Near tourist attractions

scams.name: Petition / Deaf Charity Scam
scams.description: A young woman approaches along Promenade des Anglais with a clipboard, points to her ears and mouth to signal deaf-mute, and asks whether you speak English. She wants a signature for a ‘deaf children’s charity.’ While you’re reading the clipboard, an accomplice works your bag from behind. If you sign, she flips to a donation column showing €20 and €50 contributions and becomes loud if you refuse. The charity does not exist.
scams.avoidance: Say *non merci* firmly and keep moving. Do not stop to read anything handed to you on the street — legitimate French charities do not solicit signatures from strangers. If you’re already holding the clipboard, hand it back and walk on without engaging.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Old Town, Tourist attractions, Train station

scams.name: Bird Droppings / Mustard Scam
scams.description: Something warm and wet lands on your shoulder from behind — it looks like bird droppings, or maybe squirted mustard. Within seconds, a friendly stranger materializes with tissues, tutting about the pigeons and offering to help you clean up. While you set down your bag and shrug off your jacket, their accomplice empties your pockets. The ‘droppings’ are usually paste or sauce sprayed from a concealed bottle.
scams.avoidance: If anything unexpectedly lands on you, step back from any ‘helper’ and say *non merci, ça va*. Walk into the nearest café or shop to clean up on your own. Do not set your bag down; do not take off a jacket that holds your wallet or phone. Treat the helpful stranger as part of the setup, not a coincidence.
scams.location: Busy streets, Near tourist attractions, Public squares

scams.name: Vol à la Portière (Car Door Grab)
scams.description: Thieves along the Riviera watch for rental cars — easy to spot by their stickers and foreign plates — and strike when you’re stopped at a red light or parked at a scenic turnout. They yank the passenger door open, grab whatever’s on the seat (phone on a mount, handbag, camera), and are gone on a scooter before the light changes. The French call this *vol à la portière*, and it happens fast.
scams.avoidance: Lock all doors the moment you sit down — many rentals don’t auto-lock. Keep windows up at lights and stow bags and phones on the floor behind the front seats, not on the passenger seat. Peel off the rental agency stickers where you can. Keep more space than feels natural from the car ahead so you have room to maneuver.
scams.location: Traffic lights, Car parks, Parking garages, Rental car return areas

scams.name: Rental Car Break-In
scams.description: Thieves stake out parking lots at scenic viewpoints and beach access roads, watching for rental cars by their stickers and foreign plates. They know roughly how long the average visitor spends at each attraction, so they wait for you to walk away, smash a window, and pull out whatever’s in the trunk in under a minute. France has one of the highest rates of tourist car break-ins in Western Europe.
scams.avoidance: Do not leave anything visible in the car, not even empty bags — a thief doesn’t know they’re empty. Load the trunk before you arrive, not in the lot where the thief is watching. Clear out maps, guidebooks, and rental paperwork that mark you as a visitor. Use attended parking garages when the choice is available.
scams.location: Tourist attractions, Scenic viewpoints, Parking garages, Street parking

scams.name: Fake Police Scam
scams.description: Two men in plain clothes flash what look like police badges and tell you they need to check your wallet for counterfeit bills. Sometimes a ‘lost tourist’ accomplice has just asked you to break a large note, and the ‘officer’ arrives seconds later claiming street currency exchange is illegal. While one inspects your documents, the other palms cash from your wallet. Real French police do not check tourists’ wallets on the street.
scams.avoidance: Real officers will only ask to see ID, never the wallet itself. Ask clearly to see their *carte de police* — the photo ID card with badge number — and offer to walk to the nearest *commissariat* together. Genuine police will comply; scammers won’t. Never hand over your wallet on the street, and dial 17 if something feels off.
scams.location: Tourist areas, Metro stations, Near bars at night

scams.name: Restaurant Overcharging / Water Scam
scams.description: Restaurants along Promenade des Anglais and in Vieux Nice run a familiar playbook on tourists. Waiters bring expensive bottled water when you ask for *eau*, bills include items you didn’t order, and the English menu carries higher prices than the French one. Some waiters push for ‘American-style’ tips even though service is already included, and a few refuse to seat solo diners for anything less than a full multi-course meal.
scams.avoidance: Say *une carafe d’eau, s’il vous plaît* — tap water is free by law. Ask for the French menu and compare prices line by line. Check the bill against what you ordered before paying. *Service compris* means service is already included; any additional ‘service charge’ line is not owed.
scams.location: Tourist restaurant areas, Promenade des Anglais restaurants, Old Town restaurants

scams.name: Public Transport Ticket Fine Trap
scams.description: You buy a tram or bus ticket, board, and assume you’re done. You’re not. Every ticket must be validated in the small yellow or orange machine on board — and inspectors issue €40 on-the-spot fines to anyone holding an unvalidated ticket, bought or otherwise. Drivers rarely warn about it, so tourists get caught every day.
scams.avoidance: Tap your ticket against the validator the instant you board and listen for the confirmation beep. Watch what local passengers do — the machine is small and easy to miss. If you’re not sure, ask the driver directly.

scams.name: Grand Arenas Tram Stop Pickpocket
scams.description: Grand Arenas is the stop savvy travelers use to dodge the €10 airport tram ticket — and the pickpockets know it. Teams (often teenage girls) loiter near the machines watching for tired, luggage-laden visitors. One person offers to ‘help’ you work the machine in broken English, while her partner works the other side of your bag. By the time your €1.70 ticket prints, your phone or wallet is on the far side of the platform.
scams.avoidance: Decline all offers of help at the machines with a firm *non merci*. Keep luggage in front of you, one hand on the handle and one on your bag. If you’re traveling solo, ignore anyone who approaches while you’re at the screen. The machine is simple — English is a button on the first screen.
scams.location: Grand Arenas tram stop near airport

scams.name: Rose / Flower Seller Scam
scams.description: Men with bundles of roses work the restaurant terraces along Vieux Nice, offering a ‘free’ flower for the lady. The moment either of you touches or accepts it, the price jumps to €10–€20, and they lean on the social pressure of a romantic dinner to get paid. Some sellers circle back repeatedly during the meal, betting on you paying just to make them go away.
scams.avoidance: Say *non merci* before the rose is on the table. Do not touch it — the transaction begins the moment you do. If it’s been placed down, leave it where it is and keep ignoring the seller. Ask restaurant staff to step in if he doesn’t move along. Indoor seating avoids the whole thing.
scams.location: Restaurant terraces, Promenade des Anglais, Romantic spots, Outdoor cafes

scams.name: ATM Skimming
scams.description: Criminals fit hidden card readers and fake keypads over ATM slots to capture your card data and PIN. A common variant uses a false insert that jams your card inside — when you leave to find help, the scammer returns, retrieves the card, and now has both the plastic and the code. Standalone ATMs on tourist streets are the usual targets.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside bank branches during business hours where tampering is less likely. Wiggle the card slot before inserting — skimmers tend to be loosely attached. Cover the keypad completely when entering your PIN. If your card gets stuck, do not leave the machine; call the bank number printed on it immediately. Enable transaction alerts on all travel cards before you leave home.
scams.location: Standalone ATMs, Tourist area ATMs, ATMs in dimly lit areas

scams.name: Luxury Watch Theft
scams.description: The Riviera has seen a sharp rise in thefts targeting Rolex, Patek, and Audemars Piguet wearers. Spotters cruise La Croisette equivalents and luxury hotel terraces identifying marks, then signal to riders on scooters with tampered plates who pull alongside and wrench the watch off the wrist. Others work on foot in crowded areas. The attacks can be quick, and they can turn violent if you resist.
scams.avoidance: Leave high-value watches at home or in the hotel safe — anything over €5,000 is a target on the Riviera in summer. If you must wear one, keep it under a long sleeve. Skip the conspicuous jewelry at beach clubs and on restaurant terraces, and sit with your back to a wall so no one can approach from behind. Confirm your travel insurance covers jewelry up to the item’s value before you leave home.
scams.location: Promenade des Anglais, Luxury hotel areas, Nice city center

scams.name: Vacation Rental Scam
scams.description: Scammers post fake listings on Airbnb, Vrbo, and independent rental sites, using photos stolen from real apartments and pricing them just below market to hook quick bookings. Once you wire a deposit outside the platform, the listing vanishes — and when you arrive, the address is a parking garage, the apartment belongs to someone else, or the building doesn’t exist. The Riviera sees a wave of these every summer.
scams.avoidance: Book only on the official platform and keep all payments on it — that is the only recourse you have. A wire transfer outside Airbnb is a gift you will not get back. Reverse-image-search the photos before booking. Read reviews for specific, verifiable details about the apartment, not generic praise. If the price is noticeably below comparable listings, assume it’s fake.
